source_text: Ad causam itaque referantur exempla. Ut parentum peccata filiis imputentur et parentum peccata filiis non imputentur, non potest hoc utrumque contrarium pariter iustum probari; sed si iustitia est generantium subolem ream teneri, necesse est, ut iniustitia sit, si propter eadem peccata rea non esse dicatur; et sicut bonum est iuste praecipere, ita malum est iniuste quidquam iubere; et quamvis res perspicua argumentando levior fiat, tamen, quoniam causam in absoluto positam iuvat etiam legis divinae confirmare suffragiis, inhaereamus huic loco, in quo, quicumque sana mente constiterit, per praerupta quaestionum praesentium errare non sinitur. Acquiescis igitur, annuntiator naturalis mali, praescriptum esse lege Dei, ne filii puniantur in peccatis parentum; agnoscis etiam non aliter hoc praeceptum ab illo populo intellectum fuisse, quam a nobis nunc observandum defenditur. Et ideo regem Amessiam praeceptis Dei oboedientem indignationem, quam de patris sui internecione conceperat, laudabili moderatione frenasse atque occisis parentis sui percussoribus eorum tamen filiis non per ignaviam, sed per iustitiam pepercisse. Laudatur quidem Amessias et hoc secundum Dei refertur fecisse legem commendaturque oboedisse voluntati Domini, sed tamen infuscatus vanitatis reliquiis non tacetur et ostenditur devotionem David patris sui imitatus non esse [n38] . Hic tamen ab illa generis sui sanctitate degenerans tenuit in iudicio commendatam divina lege iustitiam; tantum reverentia perspicuae aequitatis valebat. Quid ergo mali fides tua complectatur, expende: hanc iniquitatem Deo admoves, quem aeternum et pium et iustum fatemur, quam nec superbia purpurati nec dolor commisit orbati.
pass_a_gloss: Let the examples therefore be referred to the cause. That parents' sins be imputed to sons and that parents' sins not be imputed to sons—this contrary pair cannot equally be proved just; but if justice is that the offspring of those generating be held defendant, it is necessary that it be injustice if on account of the same sins it is said not to be defendant; and as it is good to precept justly, so it is evil to command anything unjustly; and although a clear thing becomes lighter by arguing, nevertheless, since it helps a cause placed in the absolute also to confirm it by the suffrages of the divine law, let us cling to this place, in which whoever has stood with a sound mind is not allowed to wander through the steeps of the present questions. You therefore acquiesce, announcer of natural evil, that it has been prescribed by the law of God that sons not be punished in the sins of parents; you also recognize that this precept was understood by that people not otherwise than as we now defend it to be observed. And therefore that king Amaziah, obeying God's precepts, by praiseworthy moderation bridled the indignation which he had conceived from the slaughter of his father, and, the strikers of his parent having been killed, nevertheless spared their sons not through cowardice but through justice. Amaziah is indeed praised and this is reported to have been done according to the law of God and he is commended to have obeyed the will of the Lord, yet he is not silent as stained with remnants of vanity and it is shown that he was not an imitator of the devotion of his father David. This man nevertheless, degenerating from that holiness of his line, held in judgment the justice commended by the divine law; so much did reverence of clear fairness avail. Weigh therefore what evil your faith embraces: you apply to God, whom we confess eternal and pious and just, this injustice which neither the pride of one clothed in purple nor the grief of one bereaved committed.

pass_b_english: Now apply these examples to the case. Charging children with their parents’ sins and not charging children with their parents’ sins cannot both be shown equally just. If justice consists in holding the offspring guilty, it must be injustice to declare them not guilty for those same sins. And just as it is good to command justly, it is evil to give an unjust order. Argument may weaken the force of something already obvious, yet it is helpful to confirm an established case by the supporting judgments of divine law. Let us stay with this point: anyone who stands here with a sound mind will not be allowed to wander among the precipices of our present disputes.

You therefore concede, preacher of natural evil, that God’s law commands that children must not be punished for their parents’ sins. You also acknowledge that this people understood the command precisely as we now maintain it should be observed. Consequently King Amaziah, obeying God’s commands, restrained with praiseworthy moderation the anger caused by his father’s murder. He killed his father’s assassins but spared their sons, out of justice, not cowardice. Amaziah is praised; he is said to have done this according to God’s law, and commended for obeying the Lord’s will. Yet the account does not conceal that remnants of false worship stained him, and it shows that he did not imitate the devotion of his ancestor David (2 Kings 14:3–6). Even this man, who fell short of his family’s holiness, maintained in judgment the justice commended by divine law. Such was the power of reverence for unmistakable fairness! Consider, then, what evil your belief embraces: you attribute to God, whom we acknowledge as eternal, good, and just, an injustice that neither a king’s pride nor a bereaved son’s grief committed.
